zone: Davis Peak — Gorge Creek and lower Stetattle Creek
_areas_note: Davis Peak alone. The catalog files it under the Picket Range and that is misleading: it stands well east of the Pickets proper, immediately north of Gorge Lake, and NOTHING about it involves Big Beaver — so none of the Northern Pickets camps apply and its id is deliberately not added there. Nor is it a Ross Lake objective; it is not approached by boat and the lake plays no part. It is a Highway 20 corridor peak, but its own trailhead is the Gorge Creek overlook between Newhalem and Diablo, several miles west of anything in the Ross Lake corridor file, so Colonial Creek Campground is NOT duplicated here and is the wrong side of Diablo Lake to be the natural base. The roadhead camps below are the ones actually near the start, plus the sleeping ground on the mountain itself.

sites.name: Gorge Creek overlook, the trailhead you sleep at
sites.capacity: A highway pullout and viewpoint parking area, not a campground. Parties routinely spend the night in a vehicle here to start at first light. There are no sites, no pitches, and nowhere to put a tent.
sites.water: Gorge Creek itself, immediately below, and it is the last certain water for a long way up. Nothing is provided at the pullout.
sites.permit: No permit and no fee to park or to sleep in a vehicle. A DAY climb from here needs no backcountry permit at all, which is the usual way this peak is done. The moment you sleep on the mountain you need a National Park Service backcountry permit for the Davis Peak cross-country zone.
sites.notes: This is where the standard scramble starts, on Highway 20 between Newhalem and Diablo. You cross the creek on the bridge and go straight into steep forest with no trail of any kind. The peak is famous for the sheer drop off its far side, and the ground you climb reflects that: expect around ten miles and roughly seven and a half thousand feet of gain, with cliff bands to be turned in the timber around twenty-four hundred and twenty-eight hundred feet and a stretch of vine maple higher. Thirteen or fourteen hours car to car is a normal time for a fit party, and that is why so many sleep at the car rather than carry overnight gear up it. Being west of the seasonal highway gate, the pullout is reachable all year, but the route wants firm snow or dry ground rather than the rotten mix in between.

sites.name: Goodell Creek Campground, Newhalem
sites.capacity: A modest road campground on the Skagit with a mix of standard sites and a couple of group sites, small enough that a busy summer weekend fills it.
sites.water: Potable water while the campground is serviced; the river is the fallback and needs treating. Availability drops off outside the main season.
sites.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No backcountry permit needed to sleep here. It has historically been the free, year-round, minimal-service option in the Newhalem cluster while the fee campgrounds close for winter — confirm the current fee and season, because the park has been adjusting both.
sites.notes: About five minutes' drive west of the Gorge Creek overlook, this is the practical base for a party that wants a real campsite the night before rather than a night in the driver's seat. It is low, forested and close to the highway, with none of the character of the alpine above it, and that is fine for its purpose. It also stays open later in the year than the larger campgrounds nearby, which matters on a peak whose best conditions are often outside the busy season. THE OBVIOUS CLOSER OPTION IS GONE: the small tent campground at Gorge Lake, right beside the creek in Diablo, has been shut for an extended period over debris-flow and flooding hazard on ground burned in an earlier fire, and should not be planned around without confirming it has reopened.

sites.name: Snowfield benches on the south side, around 4,800 feet
sites.capacity: Open ground rather than sites. Where the timber finally releases into alpine snow and slabs there is room for a small party to lie down, and no established platform to aim for.
sites.water: Running snowmelt while there is snow, which is exactly what makes this level worth stopping at. Once the slopes bare out later in summer, water here becomes unreliable and the gully lower down is the last dependable source.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required for the Davis Peak cross-country zone: six people maximum in a party, and a maximum of three parties in the zone on any night. Walk-up only, collected in person at the Marblemount wilderness office rather than reserved in advance. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and not in meadow or within a hundred feet of water. No fires anywhere in the zone. Pack waste out where the ground will not take a cathole.
sites.notes: The forest below is the whole difficulty of this mountain — steep, tangled and unrelenting, with the route picked out along animal paths and through weaknesses in the cliff bands. Getting up to this level and stopping turns a punishing single day into a manageable two, and this is the first ground on the route where a party can lie flat and see out. A partly snow-filled gully around four thousand feet is the usual way through the last of the trees onto these slopes; it is straightforward when it holds firm snow and considerably less pleasant when it is running wet or bare. Early summer is the moment for this camp, because the same snow that makes the gully work is what supplies the water.

sites.name: The 5,720 ft saddle south of the summit
sites.capacity: Room for about two small tents on a snow ledge by the saddle. That is the whole capacity, and it is not a place to plan on sharing.
sites.water: Snowmelt only, and only while snow is present at the notch. Late in a dry summer there is nothing here and everything has to be carried up from the snowfields below.
sites.permit: Same National Park Service backcountry permit and Davis Peak cross-country zone as the ground below: party of six maximum, three parties per night, walk-up from Marblemount, no fires, durable surfaces only.
sites.notes: A little over half a mile south of the summit, this notch in the ridge is the highest sensible sleeping ground on the peak and the launching point for the last of the climbing. From here the standard finish takes the rock buttress on the south ridge at easy scrambling, a couple of grades of hands-on ground rather than anything technical. Parties have also tried the broad snow slopes of the east ridge from the saddle and been stopped by a step a few hundred feet under the top, so the south side is the line to plan for. Being a saddle it is exposed to whatever the weather is doing and there is nothing to shelter behind, which argues for using it on a settled forecast and otherwise sleeping lower. NOTE THE OTHER APPROACH: the peak's steep north-east side is reached instead from the Stetattle Creek trail out of Diablo, leaving the path after a couple of miles and fording the creek — but that trail has been closed outright for falling dead trees on burned ground, so treat the Gorge Creek side as the only way in until it reopens.
